items.stem: Work done on an object is equal to …
options: force × distance moved in the direction of the force
items.answer: force × distance moved in the direction of the force
items.markingKey: W = Fd.

items.stem: Explain why work is done against friction when a box is pushed across a floor at constant speed, even though its kinetic energy does not change.
items.answer: The pushing force moves through a distance, transferring energy; this energy goes to the internal (thermal) store of the box and floor via friction, not to kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: force × distance → energy transferred [1]; goes to thermal store via friction [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain the link between work done and energy transferred when a crane lifts a load.
items.answer: The work done by the crane’s upward force (force × height) equals the gain in the load’s gravitational potential energy (plus any energy wasted).
items.markingKey: W = ΔE [1]; = gain in GPE [1] [2]

items.stem: A crane lifts a load with a steady force with a force of 2000 N through 30 m in the direction of the force. Determine the work done.
items.markingKey: W = Fd = 2000 × 30 = 60 000 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A tractor drags a log with a force of 1.5 kN through 10 m. Calculate the work done in J.
items.markingKey: convert to N and m [1]; W = Fd [1] = 15 000 J [1] [3]

items.stem: A motor lifts a 500 kg load through 8 m at a steady speed (g = 9.8 N/kg). Friction in the pulley adds a resistive force of 40 N throughout. (a) Calculate the weight of the load. (b) Calculate the work done against gravity. (c) Calculate the total work done by the motor. (d) State the gain in GPE of the load.
items.markingKey: (a) mg [1] (b) W = Fd = 4900 × 8 [1] (c) + 40 × 8 = 39 500 J [1] (d) equals work against gravity [1] [4]

items.stem: Lucas (mass 60 kg) climbs stairs of vertical height 10 m and then pushes a box with a force of 200 N for 10 m along a corridor (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) State where the energy transferred to the box ends up if the box moves at constant speed. (b) Explain why the total chemical energy used by the person is greater than the total work done. (c) State the energy store that increases when the stairs are climbed.
items.answer: (a) In the internal (thermal) store of the box, floor and air (via friction). (b) The body is not 100% efficient; much energy is transferred to the thermal store (body heat). (c) Gravitational potential.
items.markingKey: (a) In the internal (thermal) store of the box, floor and air (via friction) [1] (b) The body is not 100% efficient [1]; much energy is transferred to the thermal store (body heat) [1] [2] (c) Gravitational potential [1]

items.stem: Sofia (mass 70 kg) climbs stairs of vertical height 6 m and then pushes a box with a force of 400 N for 30 m along a corridor (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the work done against gravity in climbing the stairs. (b) Calculate the work done pushing the box. (c) State where the energy transferred to the box ends up if the box moves at constant speed. (d) State the energy store that increases when the stairs are climbed.
items.answer: (a) 4120 J (b) 12000 J (c) In the internal (thermal) store of the box, floor and air (via friction). (d) Gravitational potential.
items.markingKey: (a) W = mgh (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4120 J with unit [1] [2] (b) W = Fd: 12000 J [1] (c) In the internal (thermal) store of the box, floor and air (via friction) [1] (d) Gravitational potential [1]

items.stem: What is the unit of work done?
items.answer: joule (J)
items.markingKey: 1 J = 1 N m of work.

items.stem: A force of 50 N pushes a box 4 m along the floor. How much work is done?
A car brakes to a stop. Explain how the braking distance is related to the car’s kinetic energy.
items.answer: Work done by the braking force (F × d) equals the kinetic energy removed, so d = Eₖ/F; more kinetic energy means a longer braking distance for the same force.
items.markingKey: F × d = KE [1]; larger KE → longer distance [1] [2]

items.stem: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at constant speed. Explain whether work is done by the force named or implied.
items.answer: Gravity acts towards the centre, perpendicular to the motion, so it does no work and the KE stays constant.
items.markingKey: work needs movement in direction of force [1]; applied correctly [1] [2]

items.stem: Priya pushes a crate with a force of 20 N for 10 m and writes "work done = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 J". Identify the error, give the correct work done and state where the energy goes if the crate moves at constant speed.
items.answer: Work = force × distance, not force ÷ distance: W = 20 × 10 = 200 J. At constant speed the energy goes to the thermal store of the crate, floor and air (work against friction).
items.markingKey: W = Fd not F/d [1]; 200 J [1]; energy to thermal store via friction [1] [3]

items.stem: Sipho pushes a crate with a force of 80 N for 2 m and writes "work done = 80 ÷ 2 = 40 J". Identify the error, give the correct work done and state where the energy goes if the crate moves at constant speed.
items.answer: Work = force × distance, not force ÷ distance: W = 80 × 2 = 160 J. At constant speed the energy goes to the thermal store of the crate, floor and air (work against friction).
items.markingKey: W = Fd not F/d [1]; 160 J [1]; energy to thermal store via friction [1] [3]

items.stem: Two students of equal weight climb the same stairs; one runs and one walks. Explain who does more work and who develops more power.
items.answer: They do the same work (same weight × same height); the runner develops more power because the work is done in less time.
items.markingKey: same work [1]; runner more power, less time [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how to measure your own power when running up a flight of stairs.
items.answer: Measure your mass (weight = mg), measure the vertical height of the stairs with a tape, time the climb with a stopwatch; P = mgh/t.
items.markingKey: weight [1]; vertical height [1]; time and P = mgh/t [1] [3]

items.stem: Which equation gives efficiency in terms of power?
options: efficiency = total power input ÷ useful power output
efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input × 100%
items.answer: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input × 100%
items.markingKey: Same idea as energy efficiency, per second.

items.stem: Explain why a motor lifting a load becomes less efficient if its bearings are not lubricated.
items.answer: More friction means more of the input energy is transferred to thermal energy, so a smaller fraction becomes useful work.
items.markingKey: more friction [1]; more wasted, smaller useful fraction [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why efficiency calculated using powers gives the same result as using energies over the same time.
items.answer: Power = energy/time; for the same time both useful and input energies are divided by the same t, so the ratio is unchanged.
items.markingKey: P = E/t [1]; t cancels in ratio [1] [2]

items.markingKey: work needs movement in direction of force [1]; applied correctly [1] [2]

items.stem: A winch pulls a boat up a slipway with a force of 3000 N through 20 m in the direction of the force. Work out the work done.
items.markingKey: W = Fd = 3000 × 20 = 60 000 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Tomás pulls a suitcase through an airport in Dhaka with a force of 15 N through 175 m in the direction of the force. Determine the work done.
items.markingKey: W = Fd = 15 × 175 = 2625 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A tractor drags a log with a force of 2.8 kN through 80 m. Calculate the work done in J.
items.markingKey: convert to N and m [1]; W = Fd [1] = 224 000 J [1] [3]

items.stem: Ana (mass 60 kg) climbs stairs of vertical height 3 m and then pushes a box with a force of 300 N for 30 m along a corridor (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the work done pushing the box. (b) State where the energy transferred to the box ends up if the box moves at constant speed. (c) Explain why the total chemical energy used by the person is greater than the total work done.
items.answer: (a) 9000 J (b) In the internal (thermal) store of the box, floor and air (via friction). (c) The body is not 100% efficient; much energy is transferred to the thermal store (body heat).
items.markingKey: (a) W = Fd: 9000 J [1] (b) In the internal (thermal) store of the box, floor and air (via friction) [1] (c) The body is not 100% efficient [1]; much energy is transferred to the thermal store (body heat) [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas (mass 70 kg) climbs stairs of vertical height 6 m and then pushes a box with a force of 200 N for 20 m along a corridor (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the work done against gravity in climbing the stairs. (b) Calculate the work done pushing the box. (c) State where the energy transferred to the box ends up if the box moves at constant speed. (d) Explain why the total chemical energy used by the person is greater than the total work done.
items.answer: (a) 4120 J (b) 4000 J (c) In the internal (thermal) store of the box, floor and air (via friction). (d) The body is not 100% efficient; much energy is transferred to the thermal store (body heat).
items.markingKey: (a) W = mgh (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4120 J with unit [1] [2] (b) W = Fd: 4000 J [1] (c) In the internal (thermal) store of the box, floor and air (via friction) [1] (d) The body is not 100% efficient [1]; much energy is transferred to the thermal store (body heat) [1] [2]

items.stem: How much energy does a 2 kW heater transfer in 10 s?

Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Two students of equal weight climb the same stairs; one runs and one walks. Explain who does more work and who develops more power. (b) Explain why a more powerful car can accelerate to 100 km/h in less time than a less powerful car of the same mass.
items.answer: (a) They do the same work (same weight × same height); the runner develops more power because the work is done in less time. (b) Both need the same gain in kinetic energy; the more powerful engine transfers energy at a greater rate, so it takes less time.
items.markingKey: (a) same work [1]; runner more power, less time [1] [2] (b) same KE needed [1]; more energy per second [1] [2]

items.stem: A student compares two kettles. The energy transferred is multiplied by 5 while the time taken stays the same. Explain how the power changes.
items.answer: The power becomes 5 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using P = ΔE/t: power ∝ energy transferred; factor = 5.00 = 5.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Yusuf (mass 45 kg) runs up a staircase of vertical height 4.2 m in 5 s (g = 9.8 N/kg). Calculate Yusuf’s useful power.
A microwave oven has a power of 1200 W and is used for 5 s. Determine the energy transferred.
items.markingKey: E = Pt = 1200 × 5 = 6000 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An electric kettle has a power of 1.8 kW and is switched on for 15 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred in J.

An electric kettle rated at 1500 W heats 1.5 kg of water for 150 s. (a) Calculate the electrical energy transferred. (b) Explain what is meant by a power of 1500 W. (c) Suggest why a more powerful kettle boils the same water faster.
items.answer: (a) 225000 J (b) 1500 J of energy is transferred each second. (c) It transfers the same energy at a greater rate, so less time is needed.
items.markingKey: (a) E = Pt (method/substitution) [1]; answer 225000 J with unit [1] [2] (b) 1500 J of energy is transferred each second [1] (c) It transfers the same energy at a greater rate [1]; so less time is needed [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A 60% efficient motor has an input of 500 W. What is its useful output power? (b) A device has an efficiency of 40%. What fraction of its input is wasted?
Two pumps each take 500 W from the supply. Pump A is 90% efficient and pump B is 30% efficient. Explain which pump raises water faster and calculate the difference in useful power.
items.answer: Pump A: more useful power. Difference = 300 W.
items.markingKey: higher efficiency → more useful power from same input [1]; both useful powers [1]; difference [1] [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why efficiency calculated using powers gives the same result as using energies over the same time. (b) Describe an experiment to find the efficiency of a small electric motor lifting a mass.
items.answer: (a) Power = energy/time; for the same time both useful and input energies are divided by the same t, so the ratio is unchanged. (b) Measure input power from voltmeter and ammeter readings (P = IV) and time; measure the mass and height lifted; useful energy = mgh; efficiency = mgh ÷ (IVt) × 100%.
items.markingKey: (a) P = E/t [1]; t cancels in ratio [1] [2] (b) electrical input measured [1]; mgh measured [1]; ratio [1] [3]

items.stem: A winch motor has a useful power output of 9410 W and an input power of 15 700 W. Calculate the efficiency.
items.markingKey: efficiency = 9410/15 700 × 100 = 60%. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A pump motor raises water into a tank of mass 800 kg through 15 m in 25 s. The input power is 6000 W (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the efficiency. (b) Explain why the efficiency is less than 100%.
items.answer: (a) 78.4% (b) Energy is wasted as thermal energy (friction, resistance of coils) and sound.
items.markingKey: (a) correct method/substitution [1]; answer 78.4% with unit [1] [2] (b) Energy is wasted [1]; as thermal energy (friction, resistance of coils) and sound [1] [2]
